excerpts.why: States the late-October FOMC meeting dates (October 27-28), which fixes the event window for the thesis.
The September 2026 statement shows the Committee raised the target range, the opposite of the cut the thesis predicts.
July minutes show the Committee held rates steady, which is historical baseline context for judging a later cut.
Most September participants expected another rate increase, which weakens the case for a cut at the next meeting.
Sixteen of 18 dot-plot participants anticipated at least one more hike this year, implying a hiking rather than cutting bias.
Futures pricing shows an 85 percent chance of at least one hike, so market expectations run against a cut.
January minutes record a hold decision, which is historical background on how the Committee has been acting.
Several January participants favored downward adjustments to the target range, a dovish signal that backs the cut link.
A rising unemployment rate since mid-last-year is a labor-market weakness that could justify easing.
The labor market is described as solid and stable, which lowers the need for a rate cut.
The CPI release header provides the September 2026 inflation release context and monthly CPI rise needed to judge the policy outlook.
Headline CPI rose to 3.7 percent year over year, a rising inflation reading that argues against cutting.
Core CPI rose to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent, showing underlying inflation accelerating against a cut.
Energy prices rose 20.4 percent over the year, adding inflation pressure that weakens the case for a cut.
Waller says policy will focus on the inflation side of the mandate for the near term, which argues against easing.
Oil supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict add upward inflation pressure, reducing room for cuts.
Threatened new tariffs could push inflation up again, which argues against a near-term cut.
Strengthening activity and a stated lack of concern about tighter policy point toward holding or hiking rather than cutting.
Participants viewing the policy rate as not restrictive is ambiguous for a cut: it could mean room to ease or no need to ease.
